extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal education funds (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, and institutional legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of regulatory standards and interpretive guidance from the Department of Education's Title IX final rule preamble, focusing on appearance codes, juvenile justice facilities, burdens on schools, and the prohibition/definition of retaliation. Useful for institutions preparing policy updates, notices, or comments under the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-differentiated appearance codes subject to Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's enforcement of a sex-differentiated appearance code (including dress and grooming codes, e.g., requiring only girls to wear skirts or imposing different hair-length requirements for boys and girls) is subject to Title IX's statutory prohibition on sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recipient is barred from carrying out different treatment or separation in a manner that subjects “any person” to more than de minimis harm, except as permitted by Title IX. It is not a defense to point to a “comparably burdensome” requirement for other students or to argue that the code generally imposes “equal burdens” on both sexes; discriminating against members of both sexes does not eliminate liability (Bostock; Peltier). The Department disagrees with the “comparable burdens” test applied by some courts and considers discriminatory appearance codes sufficiently addressed by the final regulations. (Cites: Peltier, Hayden, Arnold.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to juvenile justice facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's Title IX regulations apply to juvenile justice facilities that receive Federal funds, but only to education programs or activities offered by such facilities; §106.31(a)(2) does not apply in contexts where different treatment causing more than de minimis harm is “otherwise permitted under Title IX,” including in “living facilities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While facilities have obligations (e.g., under PREA) to protect populations, generalized data and anecdotal information cited by commenters did not persuade the Department that treating youth consistent with gender identity will increase risk of rape or sexual assault so as to require regulatory change. Commenters' requests to allow placements strictly by sex assigned at birth were not adopted. Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of burdens on schools (Regulatory Impact Analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters asserted proposed §106.31(a)(2) could burden recipients by requiring construction/retrofitting for privacy, increased administrative/legal costs, monitoring, training, and recordkeeping; some might seek religious exemptions or decline federal aid to avoid application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department addresses these cost and benefit concerns in the Regulatory Impact Analysis, including costs specifically attributable to §106.31(a)(2). (No regulatory text changes were made in response beyond relying on the RIA.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation prohibited when it interferes with Title IX rights or is because of participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations prohibit retaliation that interferes with Title IX rights or that is taken because a person participated (or refused to participate) in Title IX processes; retaliation is treated as a form of sex discrimination when it is an intentional response to a complaint of sex discrimination (Jackson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition of “retaliation” in §106.2 specifies that retaliation covers only actions taken “for the purpose of interfering” with Title IX rights or “because” a person participated in the Title IX process. Title IX does not prohibit adverse actions taken for legitimate, non-retaliatory reasons; OCR will assess motive, causal connection, and whether a reason is genuine or pretextual. Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-complaints and respondents' ability to defend themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a cross-complaint by a respondent is permitted and may be consolidated with other complaints arising out of the same facts or circumstances under §106.45(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cross-complaint will not constitute retaliation provided there is another legitimate reason for the cross-complaint that is not a pretext for sex-based retaliation. The Department rejects the view that the retaliation provisions restrict a respondent's ability to defend themself if the defense is non-pretextual. Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on disciplining for false statements based solely on grievance outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations (§106.45(h)(5)) prohibit a recipient from disciplining a party, witness, or other participant for making a false statement based solely on the recipient's determination whether sex discrimination occurred in a Title IX grievance procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain discretion to discipline based on evidence other than or in addition to the outcome of the grievance procedure; however, using the determination that sex discrimination did not occur as the sole basis for concluding that someone lied is impermissible and can have a chilling effect on participation. Examples: allegations may be true but not meet the harassment standard; insufficient evidence does not equal fabrication. Changes: removed confusing 2020 framing and placed the prohibition in §106.45(h)(5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of conduct that may constitute prohibited retaliation (preamble guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although specific examples were removed from the final regulatory text, the Department's preamble explains examples of prohibited retaliation such as initiating disciplinary proceedings to deter reporting (e.g., pursuing alcohol or drug charges to dissuade reporting, disciplining a pregnant student seeking reasonable modifications), peer retaliation, and disciplining conduct that results from trauma caused by harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether specific conduct is retaliation requires close examination of facts: OCR will consider whether the recipient knew of the protected activity, causal connection to the adverse action, legitimate non-retaliatory reasons, and whether any exceptions (e.g., religious exemptions) apply. Recipients must offer and coordinate supportive measures (§106.44(g)) when they know a student may have been subject to sex discrimination. The Department removed examples from the regulatory text to avoid limiting contexts in which conduct could constitute retaliation, but discusses them in the preamble. Recipients may adopt amnesty policies but Title IX does not require them.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment protections in retaliation context
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement of Title IX is done consistent with the First Amendment; mere criticism of a recipient's policies or of a party's decision to participate in Title IX proceedings ordinarily is not retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 106.6(d) (added in 2020) and case law guide protection of speech and association; removing a statement about First Amendment protections from §106.71 was not a substantive change. A recipient-sponsored student organization must not exclude a student for the “purpose of interfering” with Title IX rights or because the person participated in the Title IX process, but such organizations may exclude for other non-pretextual reasons. The final regulations do not govern purely private groups outside a recipient's education program or activity. Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may make a retaliation complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person specified in §106.45(a)(2) has the right to make a retaliation complaint, including complainants; a parent, guardian, or authorized legal representative; the Title IX Coordinator (after making required determinations); or any student, employee, or other person participating or attempting to participate in the recipient's education program or activity at the time of alleged retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anyone who participated in the Title IX process (complainant, respondent, witness) may make a retaliation complaint if they believe adverse action was taken because of participation. Retaliation complaints by persons who did not participate are also allowed if they believe an adverse action was taken to interfere with their Title IX rights. Each complaint must be assessed on its facts to determine whether it meets the definition of retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient obligations when it has information that reasonably may constitute retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient has information about conduct that reasonably may constitute retaliation under Title IX or the part, the recipient is obligated to comply with §106.44.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under §106.44(f), the Title IX Coordinator must offer and coordinate supportive measures (which may include no-contact orders), determine whether to initiate a complaint of sex discrimination under specified circumstances, and take prompt and effective steps to ensure discrimination does not continue or recur. A recipient need not wait for a complaint to take protective action; monitoring for barriers to reporting (e.g., fear of discipline) is required and may prompt adoption of amnesty policies as an approach to address a barrier, though such policies are not mandated by Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifications to regulatory text triggering obligations and informal resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department revised regulatory text to ensure obligations are triggered whenever a recipient “has” information (not only “receives” it), and to require action when information “reasonably may constitute retaliation under Title IX or this part.” The Department also clarified that a recipient may, as appropriate and consistent with §106.44(k), offer informal resolution for retaliation complaints, and clarified consolidation language to require a postsecondary recipient to comply with both §§106.45 and 106.46.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These edits were intended to broaden the set of circumstances that trigger recipient obligations and to clarify process options (including informal resolution) for handling retaliation complaints in ways consistent with other grievance provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of “retaliation”: interference and participation clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of “retaliation” at §106.2 includes an interference clause (prohibiting an adverse action taken “for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX”) and a participation clause (applying when an adverse action is taken because a person “has reported information, made a complaint, testified, assisted, or participated or refused to participate in any manner in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing” under the Title IX regulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These clauses protect both actions that interfere with substantive or procedural Title IX rights and actions that punish or are motivated by participation in Title IX processes. The participation and interference clauses are substantially similar to parallel clauses in the Title VI retaliation provision and reflect longstanding regulatory language. OCR will evaluate motive, causal connection, and legitimacy of reasons when determining retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelled participation of employees and authorized non-employees
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's regulations do not prevent a recipient from lawfully compelling the good-faith participation of an employee or student in a Title IX proceeding, and recipients may consider whether to compel participation by authorized non-employees (e.g., volunteer coaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters raised concerns that compelling participation could conflict with Title VII practice; the Department noted differences but did not adopt an exemption for employee complainants. Institutions should balance investigatory needs with protections; recipients historically have required employee participation in Title VII contexts, and similar expectations may apply under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer retaliation explicitly covered
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department added “including peer retaliation” after “retaliation” in the first sentence of §106.71 to make clear that references to retaliation include retaliation by peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although examples of peer retaliation were removed from the regulatory paragraphs, peer retaliation remains within the scope of what the regulations prohibit and will be assessed under the same standards (motive, causal connection, legitimate reasons).
